title: Can Children Claim Property While Father Is Alive? Bangladesh Law, Gift Deeds & Senior Protection
metaTitle: Can Children Claim Property When Father Is Alive Bangladesh?
metaDescription: Understand property rights when father is alive in Bangladesh. Muslim inheritance rules, Spes Successionis, fighting forced gift deeds, and elder protection law.
keywords: can son claim father property while alive bd
heroIntro: A widespread legal dispute across families in Bangladesh arises when adult children attempt to compel an aging, living father to partition or transfer his property. Confronted with family pressure, many elderly parents ask: Can my children legally force me to divide my land while I am still alive? Can a partition suit be filed against a living father? What happens if an aggressive son coerces an elderly parent into executing a gift deed (Hiba) at the Sub-Registry Office? Senior Supreme Court Advocate Md. Shah Alam provides an authoritative judicial roadmap explaining why living parents enjoy absolute ownership under Bangladesh law and how to legally protect family estates from coercion. quickAnswer.heading: ⚡ Quick Legal Takeaway: Property Rights While Father Is Living
points: Under Muslim Law and Section 6(a) of the Transfer of Property Act 1882, children possess NO legal title or right to partition property while their father is alive. It is merely a 'Spes Successionis' (a contingent hope of succession).

Any partition suit filed by children against a living father is fatally defective and subject to immediate rejection under Order 7 Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC) for lack of cause of action.
A living father retains absolute, unfettered rights to sell, mortgage, gift (Hiba), or retain 100% of his self-acquired and ancestral property during his lifetime.

A forced or coerced gift deed executed by taking advantage of an elderly father's illness is voidable under Section 19/19A of the Contract Act and can be revoked via a civil suit under Section 39 of the Specific Relief Act 1877.
The Parents Maintenance Act, 2013 makes mental harassment, property dispossession, or abandoning elderly parents a non-bailable criminal offense punishable by imprisonment.

sections.h2: 1. The Doctrine of Spes Successionis in Bangladesh Law
sections.content:
Under Islamic jurisprudence as applied by the civil courts of Bangladesh, inheritance only opens upon the biological death of the property owner. Section 6(a) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 firmly codifies that the chance of an heir-apparent succeeding to an estate (Spes Successionis) cannot be transferred, claimed, or made the subject of any court litigation.

As long as a father is living and of sound mind, his ownership is absolute. He owes no legal duty to distribute land among his children, nor can any son or daughter demand a demarcation of boundaries or separate mutation. Any family agreement attempting to partition a living parent's land without the parent's voluntary execution is legally null and void.

sections.h2: 2. Can Children File a Partition Suit Against a Living Father?
sections.content:
One of the most frequent inquiries brought to our Supreme Court chambers involves sons filing partition suits against their fathers or siblings. The fundamental requirement of a partition lawsuit under the Partition Act, 1883 and the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 is co-ownership (unity of title and possession).

Because children hold zero co-ownership in their living father's property, they lack standing (locus standi). When a father appears in court and submits an application under Order 7 Rule 11 of the CPC for rejection of the plaint, civil courts routinely dismiss the lawsuit at the preliminary stage, often imposing exemplary compensatory costs on the litigating children.

sections.h2: 3. Lifetime Property Transfers: Rules on Valid Hiba (Gift)
sections.content:
While children cannot demand distribution, a father has full constitutional and statutory discretion to transfer property to any child or third party during his lifetime through a registered Hiba (Gift). For a Hiba to withstand judicial scrutiny in Bangladesh, three essential elements must coalesce:

  • Declaration (Ijab): A voluntary, explicit declaration by the father free from mental distress or coercion.
  • Acceptance (Qabul): Express acceptance by the recipient child.
  • Delivery of Possession (Qabdah): Actual physical or constructive transfer of possession.

Under Section 17 of the Registration Act 1908, oral gifts are no longer recognized in Bangladesh. A formal Hiba deed must be registered at the Sub-Registry Office with statutory stamp duty and registration fees.

sections.h2: 4. Challenging Coerced or Fraudulent Deeds Under Section 39 SRA
sections.content:
In real-world practice, elderly fathers in declining health are often subjected to undue influence, isolation, and fraudulent misrepresentation by ambitious children who take them to registry offices under the guise of medical paperwork. Such instruments are legally Voidable.

Under Section 39 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, an aggrieved father can institute a Title Suit for Cancellation of the Instrument in the competent Assistant Judge Court. Under Section 16 of the Contract Act 1872, where one party holds a dominant position over a frail senior, the legal burden of proof lies upon the child to prove that the deed was executed voluntarily and with independent legal advice.

sections.h2: 5. Criminal Protection: The Parents Maintenance Act 2013
sections.content:
To penalize the mistreatment of senior citizens, the Parliament of Bangladesh enacted the Parents Maintenance Act, 2013 (পিতা-মাতার ভরণপোষণ আইন, ২০১৩). Key provisions include:

  • Adult children are statutorily obligated to provide food, lodging, and healthcare to their parents.
  • Children are strictly prohibited from compelling parents to reside in old-age homes against their will.
  • Forcibly occupying a parent's residence or attempting to dispossess them constitutes a cognizable offense punishable by up to 3 months imprisonment or a fine of BDT 1,00,000.

sections.h2: 6. Protective Legal Mechanisms for Elderly Property Owners
sections.content:
Senior property owners seeking to safeguard their estates while supporting their children should implement the following courtroom-tested protections:

  1. Conditional Hiba with Life Interest: Draft the registered deed reserving full lifetime usufructuary and possession rights to the father and mother, specifying that full title vests in the child only post-demise.
  2. Refuse Irrevocable Powers of Attorney: Never execute general powers of attorney in favor of children without strict expiration terms.
  3. Emergency Injunctions: If children threaten dispossession, immediately file an injunction petition under Order 39 Rules 1 & 2 of the CPC alongside an executive petition under Section 107/144 CrPC.
